raw_text:
Sacubitril/valsartan is the first clinically successful angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI). Its rationale is dual: valsartan blocks angiotensin II type-1 receptor signaling, while sacubitril’s active metabolite inhibits neprilysin, augmenting natriuretic peptides, bradykinin and other vasoactive substrates that promote natriuresis, vasodilatation, anti-fibrosis and reverse remodeling [1]. Earlier vasopeptidase inhibition with omapatrilat suggested biological promise but was limited by angioedema, plausibly because combined ACE and neprilysin inhibition impaired bradykinin degradation; ARNI avoids ACE inhibition and requires a 36-hour washout after ACE inhibitors [2]. PARADIGM-HF was therefore designed to test whether neprilysin inhibition added to renin–angiotensin blockade could outperform enalapril in ambulatory heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) [3].

PARADIGM-HF established sacubitril/valsartan as disease-modifying therapy in chronic symptomatic HFrEF: compared with enalapril, it reduced cardiovascular death or heart-failure hospitalization, cardiovascular death, first heart-failure hospitalization and all-cause death, with more symptomatic hypotension but less renal impairment, hyperkalemia and cough [4]. Subsequent analyses clarified that mortality benefit reflected reductions in both sudden death and pump-failure death [5]. Benefit was preserved across systolic blood pressure strata, although lower pressure predicted higher absolute risk and required careful titration [6]. Patient-centered outcomes also improved: Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire scores deteriorated less with sacubitril/valsartan [7]. Recurrent-event analyses showed reductions beyond first hospitalization, strengthening the clinical relevance of the primary result [8]. Additional metabolic and congestion signals include improved glycemic control in patients with diabetes, reduced serum uric acid, and lower loop-diuretic requirements [9-11].

Implementation studies addressed the transition from trial efficacy to bedside use. TITRATION showed that gradual up-titration is feasible, particularly in patients previously receiving low-dose or no ACE inhibitor/ARB [12]. PIONEER-HF extended evidence to hospitalized patients stabilized after acute decompensated HFrEF, demonstrating larger NT-proBNP reduction than enalapril without excess renal dysfunction, hyperkalemia or angioedema [13]. TRANSITION further supported either pre-discharge or early post-discharge initiation after hemodynamic stabilization [14]. Mechanistic studies have been informative but not definitive: EVALUATE-HF did not show superiority for aortic impedance, whereas PROVE-HF linked NT-proBNP reductions with improved cardiac structure and function and showed that reverse remodeling correlated with better outcomes [15-17].

In heart failure with preserved or mildly reduced ejection fraction, the evidence is more nuanced. PARAMOUNT, a phase 2 HFpEF trial, showed greater NT-proBNP reduction versus valsartan at 12 weeks [18]. PARAGON-HF narrowly missed statistical significance for its primary endpoint overall but suggested greater benefit among patients with ejection fraction below the normal range and among women [19]. A pooled analysis across PARADIGM-HF and PARAGON-HF demonstrated that treatment effects vary continuously by ejection fraction, with benefit most evident below the higher preserved-EF range [20]. Renal analyses across the EF spectrum suggested slower eGFR decline and fewer serious renal outcomes with sacubitril/valsartan than comparator renin–angiotensin inhibition [21]. PARAGLIDE-HF, enrolling patients with EF >40% soon after worsening HF, showed greater NT-proBNP reduction versus valsartan; pooled PARAGLIDE-HF/PARAGON-HF data supported clinical benefit, particularly when EF was below normal [22,23].

Current use requires attention to phenotype and tolerability. Sacubitril/valsartan should not be combined with ACE inhibitors, is contraindicated in prior angioedema, and is limited by hypotension, renal dysfunction and hyperkalemia monitoring needs [24]. Contemporary US and European guidelines recommend ARNI as a foundational HFrEF therapy, preferably replacing ACE inhibitor/ARB in eligible symptomatic patients, and give weaker recommendations in HF with mildly reduced or preserved EF, especially at the lower EF range [25-27]. Dose-achieved analyses suggest biomarker and clinical benefit even when target dose is not reached, but titration toward 97/103 mg twice daily remains the evidence-based goal [28]. PARADIGM-HF subgroup data also argue against delaying conversion until another decompensation occurs [29]. Overall, sacubitril/valsartan has transformed HFrEF care and has a selective, EF-dependent role in HFmrEF/HFpEF; remaining questions concern sequencing with SGLT2 inhibitors and other “four-pillar” therapies, initiation in frail or advanced HF, and real-world optimization [30].
